summary: This document describes a YANG data model for the Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). The model also serves as the base for the Multipoint LDP (mLDP) model, and its modules conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).

eli5.summary: Routers using label tags need settings that tools can read. This document defines a standard form for those settings of the label-sharing protocol LDP.

questions: ldp base and extended yang modules
how to configure ldp with netconf
subtitle: A standard YANG schema for configuring, monitoring and controlling MPLS LDP on a router.

tldr.problem: Operators need a common, machine-readable way to configure and monitor the MPLS Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) on devices from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two YANG modules, a base one (ietf-mpls-ldp) and an extended one (ietf-mpls-ldp-extended). Together they cover configuration, operational state, notifications and actions, following the NMDA.
tldr.outcome: The model also serves as the base for the Multipoint LDP (mLDP) model. It covers core LDP and well-known manageability controls only, and leaves vendor-specific features to vendor augmentations.

today: RFC 9070 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text describes it as the base model for the Multipoint LDP (mLDP) YANG model.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
YANG is a modular data modeling language that NETCONF uses, and this document introduces a YANG data model for the MPLS Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) defined in RFC 5036. The model also covers LDP IPv6 (RFC 7552) and LDP capabilities (RFC 5561).

It defines four kinds of constructs: configuration, operational state, executables (actions) and notifications. The document is organized in that order.
sections.eli5: LDP is how routers tell each other which label tag to put on which kind of traffic. This document lists, in one standard form, every dial and gauge you would want for that job.

sections.title: Two Modules: Base and Extended
sections.content:
Items are split into base and extended. The base category holds the basic features of the LDP base specification and the minimum for a typical base LDP deployment. All base items are mandatory, so no if-feature is allowed in them. Examples are the LSR Id, enabling LDP interfaces and session passwords. Extended features include inbound and outbound label policies, IGP Sync and downstream on demand. LDP IPv6 is also an extended feature.

This yields two modules. ietf-mpls-ldp specifies the base features and augments the routing control-plane-protocol defined in RFC 8349, with a single allowed instance of the new identity mpls-ldp. ietf-mpls-ldp-extended specifies the extended features and augments the base module. The mLDP YANG model in turn augments both.

The text says base support will suffice for small deployments, while large deployments are expected to require both from vendors.
sections.eli5: There is a short form with the must-have questions and a longer add-on form with the fancy extras. Small networks can use just the short one.

sections.title: Scope and Modeling Choices
sections.content:
The model addresses only core LDP parameters plus widely deployed controls such as label filtering policies. Vendor-specific features belong in vendor augmentations. Multi-topology LDP (RFC 7307) is out of scope, as are applications running on top of LDP and any OAM procedures.

Other choices are worth knowing:

  • The model is VRF-centric: the default forwarding table is treated as just another VRF, and a network-instance (RFC 8529) refers to a VRF instance.
  • It supports two address families, ipv4 and ipv6.
  • It assumes a platform-wide label space (label space Id of zero); upstream-assigned labels are looked up in a Context-Specific Label Space.
  • Label and peer policies use the prefix-set and neighbor-set of the routing-policy model (RFC 9067).

The terms are used strictly: a neighbor/adjacency is an LDP-enabled LSR found by discovery, a session is a neighbor with an established TCP connection, and a peer is a session past initialization that is exchanging or ready to exchange bindings. A stale peer holds bindings kept through Graceful Restart.
sections.eli5: The authors drew a clear line around what the form covers and defined words like 'neighbor', 'session' and 'peer' carefully so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Configuration Hierarchy
sections.content:
The module sits under a network-instance, so configuration is per VRF. It is divided into global parameters, per-address-family parameters, capabilities, hello discovery, peers and forwarding. The model allows inheritance: for example, Hello holdtime can be set per VRF or per VRF interface, and a child value can override the parent.

  • Global: items such as the LSR Id. The RFC recommends a routable IPv4 unicast address as the LSR Id so legacy LDP features keep working in an IPv4 network.
  • Capabilities: disabled unless explicitly enabled, and apply to all peers in the VRF. A peer-level container can override them. The capabilities covered include Typed Wildcard FEC, End-of-LIB and Upstream Label Assignment.
  • Per-address-family: enabling LDP for a family, prefix-list label policies and the transport address.
  • Hello discovery: an interfaces container for basic discovery and a targeted container whose target list configures extended discovery to specific addresses.
  • Peers: authentication passwords and session KeepAlive timers for all or a subset of peers, and a peer list keyed by LSR Id.
  • Forwarding: for example, keeping neighbor discovery on an interface while not using it to forward MPLS packets.
sections.eli5: The settings are organized like folders: some apply to the whole router, some to one cable, some to one neighbor. A setting in a small folder can override the one in the big folder.

sections.title: Operational State
sections.content:
Read-only state lives in the same tree as the configuration, and with NMDA a query of the operational datastore returns both configured (rw) and read-only (ro) nodes. The four areas are:

  • Adjacencies: per-address-family Hello adjacencies from basic or extended discovery. For basic discovery there can be several neighbors per interface; for extended discovery there is at most one per local and target address pair.
  • Peers: session mode, authentication, KeepAlive timeout, TCP connection information, Hello adjacencies, message and binding statistics, and capability exchange.
  • Bindings: FEC-label bindings shown per FEC and address bindings shown per address, both advertised and received, with a flag for whether a label is used in forwarding.
  • Capabilities: global information and per-peer information received from the peer.

All local addresses are advertised to all peers, so no per-peer information is given for them, and a peer-centric view can be derived from what the model provides.
sections.eli5: Besides the dials, the form has gauges: who your neighbors are, which ones you are talking to, and which label tags you have handed out or received.

sections.title: Notifications and Actions
sections.content:
The model defines notifications for important events such as changes in the operational state of an LDP peer, a Hello adjacency or a FEC. An LDP FEC counts as up as long as it has at least one Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (NHLFE) with an outgoing label.

It also defines RPC actions, for example to clear (reset) LDP peers, hello-adjacencies and statistics. Control is graded so a user can clear everything, everything of one type, or one specific entity.
sections.eli5: The model includes a doorbell that rings when something important changes, and reset buttons that can restart everything, a group, or just one neighbor.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The model inherits the security considerations of RFC 5920 and the LDP specifications it builds on. Access to the data is via NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040), with SSH and TLS as the mandatory-to-implement secure transports, and access can be restricted with NACM (RFC 8341).

Writable nodes are sensitive: changing LDP configuration may allow the entire MPLS LDP domain to be compromised. Some RPCs are sensitive too, namely mpls-ldp-clear-peer and mpls-ldp-clear-hello-adjacency, because uncontrolled access could cause control plane flaps, network outages and DoS attacks. Implementations must rate-limit notifications to avoid significant load and side effects on system stability.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change these settings can mess up the whole label network, so only trusted people should get the keys, and the doorbell must not ring too often.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: Two URIs were registered in the IETF XML Registry: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-mpls-ldp and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-mpls-ldp-extended. The two modules were registered in the YANG Module Names registry with the prefixes ldp and ldp-ext respectively.
sections.eli5: Both forms were given official names in a public list so nobody else uses the same names.
